# Morse Documentation — Complete
# Morse is an open, decentralized headless CMS protocol built on Sui and Walrus.
# Index: https://docs.morsecms.xyz/llms.txt · Site: https://docs.morsecms.xyz/
# Feedback: https://github.com/arcadiasystems/morse-dcms/issues/new?labels=docs-feedback

<!-- Source: https://docs.morsecms.xyz/index.html -->

# Morse - The Decentralized Headless CMS Protocol

> A headless CMS protocol built on Sui and Walrus, for developers building content applications with on-chain ownership and decentralized storage.

> **WARNING: Testnet status**
>
> Morse runs on **Sui testnet only** and the contracts are **unaudited**. Sui and Walrus testnets reset periodically (Walrus wipes every few months) - stored content and object IDs are lost on reset. Testnet SUI and WAL have no monetary value. Don't publish anything you can't afford to lose.

## What is Morse?

Morse lets developers build content applications - blogs, knowledge bases, gated media platforms - where the backend is an open protocol instead of a vendor service. You define content structures, set access policies, and publish through a CLI or TypeScript SDK; the contracts handle identity, permissions, and revision history so there is no central point of failure to trust or migrate away from.

## Why Morse?

Traditional headless CMSs create several long-term constraints:

- **Trust concentration** - one vendor backend controls all identity and data
- **Weak portability** - publication identity and permissions don't travel with you
- **Opaque history** - change and authorization history is hidden inside a closed system
- **Vendor lock-in** - migrating requires re-building your backend from scratch

Morse solves these while keeping the ergonomics of headless CMS architecture. Publication identity is canonical on-chain. Write permissions are capability-based and verifiable. Every revision is auditable. And any team can integrate directly with the contracts, bypassing any specific service provider.

## System Architecture

Morse is composed of five layers. Only the contracts are the source of truth; all other layers are replaceable.

- **Control**: Sui Blockchain · Publication Registry · Collections · Entries & Revisions · OwnerCap / PublisherCap
- **Storage**: Walrus · Blob Storage · Quilt Storage
- **Access**: Seal · Publisher Policy · Allowlist Policy
- **Query**: Indexer · Content API
- **Develop**: TypeScript SDK · CLI

## Key Features

- **On-chain Permission Management** — Publication identity, write permissions, and state transitions are enforced by Move smart contracts - transparent and auditable.
- **Walrus Storage** — Content payloads and assets live in Walrus decentralized storage. Contracts store verifiable references, not bytes.
- **Capability-Based Auth** — OwnerCap and PublisherCap separate permission management from publishing. Revocation is instant and denylist-based.
- **Immutable Revisions** — Every content change is an appended revision. Draft and public heads enable editorial workflows without losing history.
- **Access Policies** — Public, publisher-gated, and subscription access policies control payload retrieval via Seal encryption.
- **Open Protocol** — Anyone can build integrations directly on contracts. Off-chain services are optional ergonomics, not gatekeepers.
- **Agent-First by Design** — A coding agent can provision publications, publish content, and operate the entire backend via CLI or SDK - no centralized provisioning required.

## Component Status

| Component | Status | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Move Contracts** | Active | Publication, collection, entry, and revision management. Deployed on Sui Testnet. |
| **TypeScript SDK** | Active | Wraps Sui, Walrus, and Seal behind a small adapter pattern. Published as `@arcadiasystems/morse-sdk` on npm (testnet). |
| **CLI** | Active | Terminal tool for managing publications, collections, and entries. Published as `@arcadiasystems/morse-cli` on npm (testnet). |
| **Indexer** | Planned | Listens to on-chain events and builds read-optimized state. |
| **Content API** | Planned | REST API for querying publications, collections, and entries. |

## Next Steps

- [Quick Start](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start.html): Choose your path - CLI, SDK, or contracts - and go from zero to published content on testnet.
- [Live Demo](https://morse-blog-demo.vercel.app): A working blog running on Morse - wallet-native publishing, on-chain revisions, Seal-gated premium posts. No wallet needed to read.
- [Core Concepts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/core-concepts.html): Understand the Publication → Collection → Entry model.
- [CLI](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/cli-overview.html): Manage publications and content from your terminal. Encrypted keystore, active context, no IDs to paste.
- [SDK](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-overview.html): Build on Morse from Node or the browser. Adapter pattern, branded IDs, structured errors.

# Core Concepts

> Understand the fundamental building blocks of the Morse protocol - the data model, authorization system, storage strategy, and how on-chain and off-chain components interact.

## The Data Model

Morse organizes content in a four-level hierarchy. Each level is stored on-chain and has a clear responsibility:

- **Level 1**: Publication
- **Level 2**: Collection
- **Level 3**: Entry
- **Level 4**: Revision

### A Concrete Example

Imagine you run a team blog. Here's how it maps to the Morse data model:

- **Publication** `team-blog` - your brand-level content domain, registered with a unique slug
- **Collection** `articles` - one content lane for blog posts (blob mode, since each post is independent)
- **Entry #0** `welcome-post` - your first blog post, assigned the monotonic ID `0`
- **Revision 0** - the initial published version. `public_head` points here, so readers see it immediately
- **Revision 1** - an updated draft. `draft_head` points here, but `public_head` still points to revision 0 - readers see the original until you explicitly promote the draft

Editors operate mostly at the **Entry / Revision** level. Owners operate mostly at the **Publication / Authorization** level.

## Publications

Think of a publication as your project or site - it is the top-level namespace that groups all your content together. Every publication gets a unique slug (like `my-blog`) that acts as a human-readable identifier across the protocol. All collections, entries, and permissions live under this single umbrella.

[See Publications for the full reference →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/publications.html)

## Collections

Collections are how you organize entries within a publication - similar to folders or content types. For example, a blog might have an `articles` collection and a `site-pages` collection. When you create a collection, you choose how its content is stored: individually as separate blobs (good for standalone posts or images) or as a shared document that can be patched in place (good for structured data like settings or configuration).

[See Collections for the full reference →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/collections.html)

## Entries & Revisions

Entries are the actual content pieces - a blog post, an image, a page. Every edit creates a new revision rather than overwriting the previous one, giving you a complete version history whose on-chain record is immutable. The system tracks two pointers for each entry: a draft head for work-in-progress and a public head that readers see. This lets drafts evolve privately while production clients serve stable published content.

[See Entries for the full reference →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/entries.html)

## How Publishing Works

End-to-end flow when you publish content:

1. **Authenticate** - hold a `PublisherCap` for the target publication
2. **Upload** - upload content bytes to Walrus, get a blob reference
3. **Register** - create an entry on-chain storing the blob reference, content type, and access policy
4. **Heads update** - public_head and/or draft_head update based on encryption status
5. **Read** - any client resolves the entry and fetches the payload from Walrus

## Capability-Based Authorization

Instead of usernames and passwords, Morse uses on-chain capability objects to manage permissions. Owning the right object in your wallet proves you have permission to act - no login server required. Morse separates ownership from publishing using two types of capability tokens. An `OwnerCap` (one per publication) controls administrative operations like issuing permissions and deleting the publication. `PublisherCap`s (many per publication) grant write access and are bound to a specific holder address.

Revocation uses a denylist-based model - issuing caps is cheap (zero table writes), and only revocations write to the denylist. Once revoked, all future writes using that cap are immediately rejected.

[See Access Control for the full reference →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/access-control.html)

## Walrus Storage

The Sui blockchain only stores references (pointers) to your content, not the content bytes themselves. The actual payloads live on Walrus, a decentralized storage network designed for large data. This separation keeps on-chain costs low while keeping your content verifiable: payloads stay available for the storage period you fund (measured in Walrus epochs) and can be renewed at any time. Walrus is format-agnostic, so Morse can support JSON, Markdown, images, video, or any custom schema.

[See Collections → Storage Modes for storage mode details →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/collections.html#storage-modes)

## Access Control

Morse can gate content behind on-chain encryption using Seal. Only users who meet specific on-chain conditions can decrypt and read the content. This means access rules are enforced by the blockchain itself, not by a server you have to trust. This approach enables paid subscriptions, token-gated access, team-only content, and other models - all without a centralized gatekeeper.

[See Access Control for the full reference →](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/access-control.html)

## Off-Chain Services

The blockchain is the canonical source of truth, but off-chain services improve the developer experience. Morse provides optional infrastructure like an indexer (for fast search and queries) and a content API (for read access) so you do not have to query the chain directly. These services make building apps on Morse faster and simpler, but they are not required.

- **Indexer** - listens to on-chain events and builds a read-optimized state database
- **Content API** - serves fast queries for listings, slug resolution, and payload references
- **SDK** - TypeScript package that wraps Sui/Walrus/Seal interactions for app developers
- **CLI** - command-line tool for scripted automation, CI, and agent-native workflows

Importantly, all off-chain services are replaceable. Any team can run their own indexer, API, or integrate directly with the contracts via the SDK. Protocol access is never gated by a single service provider.

## Next Steps

- [Quick Start](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start.html): Choose CLI, SDK, or Smart Contracts and go from zero to published content on testnet.
- [Publications](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/publications.html): Full reference for the top-level content container: slugs, capabilities, and lifecycle.
- [Collections](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/collections.html): Storage modes, entry IDs, and collection management.
- [Access Control](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/access-control.html): OwnerCap, PublisherCap, revocation, and Seal encryption.

# Quick Start

> Choose the path that fits your workflow. Each guide takes you from zero to published content on testnet.

> **INFO: New to Morse?**
>
> Start with [Core Concepts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/core-concepts.html) for an overview, or jump straight into the CLI guide. It is the fastest way to see Morse in action.

- [CLI](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-cli.html): Install morse-cli from npm, create a publication, publish and read content, all from your terminal. For operators and content managers. *(~5 min · Bun or Node · funded Sui wallet)*
- [TypeScript SDK](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-sdk.html): Wire up @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk, create a publication, add an entry and read it back in a single script. For app developers building on Morse. *(~5 min · Bun or Node · funded Sui wallet)*
- [Smart Contracts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-contracts.html): Interact with Morse's deployed contracts directly via PTBs. For developers who want full control over transaction construction. *(~10 min · Sui CLI · funded Sui wallet)*

## Every path needs a funded testnet wallet

All three guides sign transactions on Sui testnet and store content on Walrus testnet. You need SUI for gas and WAL for storage. Both are free and take about two minutes.

| Step | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Install a wallet | Sui Wallet, Suiet, or any Sui-compatible wallet | Holds your key and signs transactions |
| 2. Get testnet SUI | [faucet.sui.io](https://faucet.sui.io/) | Gas for every on-chain action |
| 3. Swap some SUI for WAL | [stake-wal.wal.app](https://stake-wal.wal.app/?network=testnet) | Walrus storage fees when you publish |

> **WARNING: Testnet only, for now**
>
> Contracts are unaudited and testnets reset periodically. Testnet tokens have no monetary value. Mainnet is on the [roadmap](https://www.morsecms.xyz/#roadmap).

<!-- Source: https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-cli.html -->

# Quick Start: CLI

> Install morse-cli and go from zero to published content on testnet in under five minutes. No contracts, no code, just your terminal.

- About 5 minutes
- Bun or Node
- Funded Sui wallet
- Sui testnet

> **WARNING: Testnet status**
>
> Morse runs on **Sui testnet only** and the contracts are **unaudited**. Sui and Walrus testnets reset periodically (Walrus wipes every few months), so stored content and object IDs are lost on reset. Testnet SUI and WAL have no monetary value. Do not publish anything you cannot afford to lose.

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Details | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bun or Node | v1.2+ / ≥ 18 | JavaScript runtime |
| Sui wallet | Sui Wallet, Suiet, or any Sui-compatible wallet | Signing transactions on testnet |
| SUI + WAL tokens | [SUI faucet](https://faucet.sui.io/) · [Swap SUI for WAL](https://stake-wal.wal.app/?network=testnet) | Gas fees (SUI) and Walrus storage fees (WAL) |
| Bech32 private key | A `suiprivkey1...` string | CLI authentication. Export from your wallet's settings |

## Installing

Install the CLI globally using your preferred package manager.

```bash
npm i -g @arcadiasystems/morse-cli
```

```bash
bun add -g @arcadiasystems/morse-cli
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
morse --help
```

## Creating a profile

A profile stores your network, RPC endpoint and active context. Create one for testnet:

```bash
morse config add testnet --network testnet
```

Verify your profile is active:

```bash
morse status
```

## Importing your key

Import a Sui private key into the encrypted keystore. The CLI prompts interactively for the key and a password. Keys are never passed as flags.

```bash
morse account import
```

> **INFO: Key format**
>
> Paste a Bech32 `suiprivkey1...` string. Export one from your wallet's settings. For non-interactive environments (CI, scripts), set `MORSE_PRIVATE_KEY` instead; the CLI uses it directly and skips the keystore prompt.

## Creating a publication

This creates a publication with a globally unique slug and auto-selects it as the active context.

```bash
morse publication create --name "My Blog" --slug "my-blog-$(date +%s)"
```

> **INFO: Slugs are globally unique**
>
> Like usernames, a slug can only be registered once on the whole network. The timestamp suffix keeps this command collision-free for everyone following this guide. For a real project, pick any unused slug. If a slug is taken, the transaction aborts with `ESlugAlreadyExists`.

```output
Creating "My Blog"...
Created "My Blog" (0x23d2...)
  ownerCap:     0xa40a...
  publisherCap: 0x6141...
  tx:           7nF2n...
Selected as the active publication.
```

> **INFO: Which IDs to save**
>
> The CLI auto-selects new publications and collections as your active context, so you rarely need to paste IDs. If you need them later, run `morse status` to see your active publication ID and collection.

## Creating a collection

Collections group entries within a publication. The CLI auto-selects the new collection as your active context, so subsequent entry commands target it automatically.

```bash
morse collection create posts
```

```output
Creating collection "posts" (blob)...
Created collection "posts".
Selected as the active collection. (tx: DWkD...)
```

## Publishing an entry

Create a content file and publish it. The CLI uploads the file to Walrus and registers the entry on-chain.

> **WARNING: This step needs WAL, not just SUI**
>
> Everything up to here only cost SUI gas. Uploading to Walrus also spends WAL. Make sure your account holds both before running this (swap SUI for WAL at [stake-wal.wal.app](https://stake-wal.wal.app/?network=testnet)), or the upload fails with `Insufficient WAL balance`.

```bash
echo '{"title": "Hello World", "body": "My first post on Morse."}' > post.json
```

Publish it. The CLI targets the active publication and collection by default. You can override with `-P <slug|id>` and `-C <name>`:

```bash
morse entry add hello --file post.json
```

```output
Uploading 65 bytes to Walrus...
✔ Added entry #0 "hello" (tx: D9Yfjk...)
  view: https://aggregator.walrus-testnet.walrus.space/v1/blobs/0iKeii...
```

## Reading it back

Fetch the entry content by its ID. Entry IDs are monotonic; your first entry is `0`.

```bash
morse entry read 0 --via-aggregator
```

The optional `--via-aggregator` flag routes reads through the Walrus aggregator, which is more reliable on testnet. Without it, testnet reads frequently fail with `No valid blob metadata could be retrieved from any storage node`, especially right after an upload. See [CLI Cookbooks → Reading It Back](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/cli-workflows.html#reading-it-back).

```output
{"title": "Hello World", "body": "My first post on Morse."}
```

> **TIP: You are live on-chain**
>
> Your content is stored on Walrus and registered on Sui testnet. Run `morse status` to see your active context, or `morse entry list` to see all entries in the collection. If you hit errors at any step, run `morse --help` or see the [CLI Cookbooks](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/cli-workflows.html#troubleshooting) troubleshooting section.

## Next steps

- [CLI: Command Reference](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/cli-commands.html): Every command and flag: publication, collection, entry, revision, cap.
- [CLI: Cookbooks](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/cli-workflows.html): Multi-step recipes: encrypted entries, multi-writer setups, CI/CD scripting.
- [Core Concepts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/core-concepts.html): The data model: publications, collections, entries and revisions.

# Quick Start: SDK

> Create a publication, add an entry, and read it back in one TypeScript script. Server-side with KeypairAdapter - no browser, no wallet popups. Want to see the result first? Browse the [live demo blog](https://morse-blog-demo.vercel.app) built on this SDK.

> **WARNING: Testnet status**
>
> Morse runs on **Sui testnet only** and the contracts are **unaudited**. Sui and Walrus testnets reset periodically (Walrus wipes every few months) - stored content and object IDs are lost on reset. Testnet SUI and WAL have no monetary value. Don't publish anything you can't afford to lose.

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Details | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bun or Node | v1.2+ / >= 18 | JavaScript runtime |
| SUI + WAL tokens | [SUI faucet](https://faucet.sui.io/) / [Swap SUI for WAL](https://stake-wal.wal.app/?network=testnet) | Gas fees (SUI) and Walrus storage fees (WAL) |
| Bech32 private key | A `suiprivkey1...` string | SDK authentication - export from your wallet's settings |

## Installing

Install the SDK and its peer dependencies using your preferred package manager. See [SDK Client Setup → Compatibility](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html#compatibility) for compatible dependency versions.

With Bun:

```bash
bun add @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk @mysten/sui@2.16.2 @mysten/walrus@1.1.6 @mysten/seal@1.1.3
```

Or with npm:

```bash
npm install @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk @mysten/sui@2.16.2 @mysten/walrus@1.1.6 @mysten/seal@1.1.3
```

Or with Yarn:

```bash
yarn add @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk @mysten/sui@2.16.2 @mysten/walrus@1.1.6 @mysten/seal@1.1.3
```

`@mysten/sui` is a required peer dependency. `@mysten/walrus` is needed for the `DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter` used below. `@mysten/seal` is required at runtime even for non-encrypted workflows.

## Writing the Script

Save this as `quickstart.ts`. It creates a publication, adds a collection, uploads an entry, and reads it back.

> **INFO: Transport: gRPC**
>
> This guide uses `SuiGrpcClient` from `@mysten/sui/grpc` - the SDK's client interfaces are typed against it. The JSON-RPC `SuiClient` from `@mysten/sui/client` is not supported; a JSON-RPC fallback is planned but has not shipped yet. See [SDK Client Setup](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html) for details.

```typescript
import { SuiGrpcClient } from "@mysten/sui/grpc";
import { Ed25519Keypair } from "@mysten/sui/keypairs/ed25519";
import {
  KeypairAdapter,
  morseConfig,
  RpcPublicationReader,
  createPublication,
  createCollection,
  addEntryFromBytes,
  DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter,
  HttpAggregatorReadAdapter,
} from "@arcadiasystems/morse-sdk";

const privateKey = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;
if (!privateKey) throw new Error("Set PRIVATE_KEY to a suiprivkey1... Bech32 string");

// 1. Configure client and adapter
const config = morseConfig({ network: "testnet" });
const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
  network: "testnet",
  baseUrl: config.rpcUrl,
});
const keypair = Ed25519Keypair.fromSecretKey(privateKey);
const adapter = KeypairAdapter.fromSecretKey(privateKey, client);
const reader = RpcPublicationReader.fromMorseConfig(config, client);

// 2. Create a publication
const pub = await createPublication(adapter, config, {
  name: "My Publication",
  slug: `my-pub-${Date.now()}`, // slugs are globally unique on-chain
});
console.log("Publication:", pub.publicationId);

// 3. Add a collection
await createCollection(adapter, config, {
  publicationId: pub.publicationId,
  publisherCapId: pub.publisherCapId,
  name: "posts",
  storageMode: "blob",
});
console.log("Collection created: posts");

// 4. Upload and add an entry
const walrusWriter = DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter.fromConfig(
  { network: "testnet", suiClient: client },
  keypair,
);

const entry = await addEntryFromBytes(adapter, config, {
  walrus: walrusWriter,
  publicationId: pub.publicationId,
  publisherCapId: pub.publisherCapId,
  collectionName: "posts",
  name: "first-post",
  bytes: new TextEncoder().encode(
    JSON.stringify({ title: "Hello World", body: "My first post on Morse." })
  ),
  contentType: "application/json",
  upload: { epochs: 3, deletable: true },
});
console.log("Entry ID:", entry.entryId);

// 5. Read it back (metadata from Sui, content from Walrus)
const fetched = await reader.getEntry(
  pub.publicationId,
  "posts",
  entry.entryId,
);
console.log("Entry name:", fetched.name);
console.log("Revisions:", fetched.revisions.length);

const walrusReader = HttpAggregatorReadAdapter.fromMorseConfig(config, client);
const content = await walrusReader.readBlobRef(fetched.revisions[0].blobRef);
console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(content));
```

`HttpAggregatorReadAdapter` routes content reads through the Walrus aggregator, which is more reliable on testnet. See [SDK Client Setup → Picking a Walrus Adapter](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html#picking-a-walrus-adapter) for alternatives.

> **TIP: Which IDs to save**
>
> The return values (`pub.publicationId`, `pub.publisherCapId`, `entry.entryId`) contain everything you need for subsequent calls. Log them or store them in your app's config.

## Running It

With Bun:

```bash
PRIVATE_KEY="suiprivkey1..." bun run quickstart.ts
```

With Node (requires `"type": "module"` in your `package.json` for top-level `await`):

```bash
PRIVATE_KEY="suiprivkey1..." npx tsx quickstart.ts
```

```output
Publication: 0x1a2b...3c4d
Collection created: posts
Entry ID: 0
Entry name: first-post
Revisions: 1
```

> **TIP: You're live on-chain**
>
> Your publication, collection, and entry are on Sui testnet. The entry content is stored on Walrus. For browser integration with wallet popups, see [SDK Client Setup -> Browser](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html#browser-setup).

- [SDK: Client Setup](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html): Browser setup, wallet adapters, Walrus adapter options, and error handling.
- [SDK: Cookbooks](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-workflows.html): Encrypted entries, revisions, reading content, and the full publishing API.
- [Core Concepts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/core-concepts.html): Understand the data model - publications, collections, entries, and revisions.

# Quick Start: Smart Contracts

> Create a publication, add a collection, and publish an entry using raw Programmable Transaction Blocks against the deployed Morse contracts on testnet. No SDK wrappers - just `tx.moveCall`.

> **WARNING: Testnet status**
>
> Morse runs on **Sui testnet only** and the contracts are **unaudited**. Sui and Walrus testnets reset periodically (Walrus wipes every few months) - stored content and object IDs are lost on reset. Testnet SUI and WAL have no monetary value. Don't publish anything you can't afford to lose.

## Prerequisites

| Requirement | Details | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bun or Node | v1.2+ / >= 18 | JavaScript runtime |
| SUI + WAL tokens | [SUI faucet](https://faucet.sui.io/) / [Swap SUI for WAL](https://stake-wal.wal.app/?network=testnet) | Gas fees (SUI) and Walrus storage fees (WAL) |
| Bech32 private key | A `suiprivkey1...` string | Transaction signing - export from your wallet's settings |

## Installing

Install the Morse SDK (for network configuration and Walrus uploads) and the Sui SDK (for transaction construction and signing).

With Bun:

```bash
bun add @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk @mysten/sui @mysten/walrus @mysten/seal
```

Or with npm:

```bash
npm install @arcadiasystems/morse-sdk @mysten/sui @mysten/walrus @mysten/seal
```

> **INFO: Why the SDK if we're using raw PTBs?**
>
> This guide uses raw `tx.moveCall` - no SDK wrappers for contract calls. The SDK packages provide three things:  `morseConfig` - resolves the deployed package ID, registry ID, and RPC URL so you don't hard-code addresses `DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter` - handles blob uploads to Walrus (requires `@mysten/walrus`) `DefaultSealAdapter` - handles Seal encryption (requires `@mysten/seal`, loaded at runtime even for non-encrypted workflows)  For the high-level wrapper approach, see the [SDK Quick Start](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-sdk.html).

## Writing the Script

Save this as `quickstart-contracts.ts`. It creates a publication, adds a collection, uploads content to Walrus, and registers an on-chain entry - all using raw PTBs.

> **INFO: Transport: gRPC**
>
> This guide uses `SuiGrpcClient` for its typed interface and lower latency. The Morse SDK also supports JSON-RPC via `SuiHTTPTransport` from `@mysten/sui/client` if your environment requires it - see [SDK Client Setup](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/sdk-client-setup.html) for details.

```typescript
import { SuiGrpcClient } from "@mysten/sui/grpc";
import { Transaction } from "@mysten/sui/transactions";
import { Ed25519Keypair } from "@mysten/sui/keypairs/ed25519";
import { bcs } from "@mysten/sui/bcs";
import { morseConfig, DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter } from "@arcadiasystems/morse-sdk";

const privateKey = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;
if (!privateKey) throw new Error("Set PRIVATE_KEY to a suiprivkey1... Bech32 string");

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 1. Configure client, keypair, and Walrus adapter
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
const config = morseConfig({ network: "testnet" });
const PACKAGE_ID = config.packageId;
const REGISTRY_ID = config.registryId;

const client = new SuiGrpcClient({
  network: "testnet",
  baseUrl: config.rpcUrl,
});
const keypair = Ed25519Keypair.fromSecretKey(privateKey);
const walrusWriter = DefaultWalrusWriteAdapter.fromConfig(
  { network: "testnet", suiClient: client },
  keypair,
);

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 2. Create a publication
//    new_publication returns (Publication, OwnerCap, PublisherCap).
//    Share the publication and transfer the caps in the same PTB.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
const pubTx = new Transaction();

const created = pubTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::new_publication`,
  arguments: [
    pubTx.object(REGISTRY_ID),
    pubTx.pure.string("My Blog"),
    pubTx.pure.string(`my-blog-${Date.now()}`), // slugs are globally unique on-chain
  ],
});

// Share the publication so other transactions can reference it.
pubTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::share_publication`,
  arguments: [created[0]],
});

// Transfer caps using typed wrappers (key-only objects can't use transferObjects).
pubTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::transfer_owner_cap`,
  arguments: [created[1], pubTx.pure.address(keypair.toSuiAddress())],
});
pubTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::transfer_publisher_cap`,
  arguments: [created[2], pubTx.pure.address(keypair.toSuiAddress())],
});

const pubResult = await client.signAndExecuteTransaction({
  transaction: pubTx,
  signer: keypair,
  include: { effects: true, objectTypes: true },
});

// Extract created object IDs from transaction effects.
const { effects, objectTypes } = pubResult.Transaction;
const createdObjects = effects.changedObjects
  .filter((c) => c.idOperation === "Created" && objectTypes?.[c.objectId])
  .map((c) => ({ objectId: c.objectId, type: objectTypes[c.objectId] }));

const PUBLICATION_ID = createdObjects.find((o) => o.type.includes("Publication"))!.objectId;
const OWNER_CAP_ID = createdObjects.find((o) => o.type.includes("OwnerCap"))!.objectId;
const PUBLISHER_CAP_ID = createdObjects.find((o) => o.type.includes("PublisherCap"))!.objectId;

console.log("Publication:", PUBLICATION_ID);
console.log("OwnerCap:", OWNER_CAP_ID);
console.log("PublisherCap:", PUBLISHER_CAP_ID);

// Wait for the transaction to be indexed before referencing the new objects.
await client.waitForTransaction({ digest: pubResult.Transaction.digest });

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 3. Add a collection
//    Blob mode (storage_mode = 0): each entry holds a standalone Walrus Blob.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
const colTx = new Transaction();

colTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::create_collection`,
  arguments: [
    colTx.object(PUBLICATION_ID),
    colTx.object(PUBLISHER_CAP_ID),
    colTx.pure.string("posts"),
    colTx.pure.u8(0),  // STORAGE_MODE_BLOB
  ],
});

const colResult = await client.signAndExecuteTransaction({ transaction: colTx, signer: keypair });
console.log("Collection created: posts");

// Wait for the collection transaction to be indexed before modifying the publication again.
await client.waitForTransaction({ digest: colResult.Transaction.digest });

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// 4. Upload content to Walrus and add an entry
//    Upload returns the Blob *object* ID (a Sui object reference).
//    Pass it via tx.object()  - the contract takes &Blob, not the hash.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
const content = new TextEncoder().encode(
  JSON.stringify({ title: "Hello World", body: "My first post on Morse." })
);
const { blobObjectId: BLOB_OBJECT_ID } = await walrusWriter.uploadBlob(content, {
  epochs: 3,
  deletable: true,
});
console.log("Blob uploaded:", BLOB_OBJECT_ID);

// BCS-encode Option<vector<u8>>::None for quilt_patch_id and seal_id.
const optionNone = bcs.option(bcs.vector(bcs.u8())).serialize(null).toBytes();

const entryTx = new Transaction();

entryTx.moveCall({
  target: `${PACKAGE_ID}::publication::add_entry_to_collection`,
  arguments: [
    entryTx.object(PUBLICATION_ID),     // &mut Publication
    entryTx.object(PUBLISHER_CAP_ID),   // &PublisherCap
    entryTx.pure.string("posts"),       // collection name
    entryTx.pure.string("hello-world"),  // entry name
    entryTx.object(BLOB_OBJECT_ID),     // blob: &Blob (must be deletable)
    entryTx.pure(optionNone),           // quilt_patch_id: None (blob mode)
    entryTx.pure.string("application/json"), // content type
    entryTx.pure.bool(false),           // encrypted: false
    entryTx.pure.u8(0),                // access_policy: PUBLIC
    entryTx.pure(optionNone),           // seal_id: None
  ],
});

await client.signAndExecuteTransaction({ transaction: entryTx, signer: keypair });
console.log("Entry added: hello-world (ID 0)");
```

> **TIP: Which IDs to save**
>
> Save the Publication, OwnerCap, and PublisherCap object IDs from the output - you need them for all subsequent contract calls. You can also recover the publication ID from its slug using `get_publication_id_by_slug` on the registry.

## Running It

```bash
PRIVATE_KEY="suiprivkey1..." bun run quickstart-contracts.ts
```

```output
Publication: 0x1a2b...3c4d
OwnerCap: 0x5e6f...7a8b
PublisherCap: 0x9c0d...1e2f
Collection created: posts
Blob uploaded: 0x4d5e...6f7a
Entry added: hello-world (ID 0)
```

> **TIP: You're live on-chain**
>
> Your publication, collection, and entry are on Sui testnet. The entry content is stored on Walrus. For a friendlier reading experience, use the [Morse CLI](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/quick-start-cli.html): `morse entry read 0 --via-aggregator`.

## Next Steps

- [Contract Cookbooks](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/contracts-workflows.html): Revisions, drafts, encrypted content, delegating access, and teardown  - all via raw PTBs.
- [Contract Reference](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/contracts-reference.html): Full function signatures, argument types, error codes, and Move struct definitions.
- [Core Concepts](https://docs.morsecms.xyz/core-concepts.html): Understand the data model  - publications, collections, entries, and revisions.
